SIBAWAYH: Sībawayh distinguishes verbal-noun or direction expressions such as forward and back from place names, which instead involve an omitted preposition. SIBAWAYH: ʿĀmir ibn al-Ṭufayl's line uses place names; the intended sense includes the preposition bi, unlike the verbal-noun examples. SIBAWAYH: In expressions such as back and belly or plain and mountain, the second noun may be nominative as apposition or emphasis, or accusative in an expanded construction. SIBAWAYH: The implied sense is on the back and belly or in the plain and mountain; this is not ordinary adverbial syntax and is restricted to established pairs. SIBAWAYH (الخليل): Khalīl reports the idiom مطرنا الزرع والضرع; Sībawayh allows its second nouns to be parsed as apposition, emphasis, or accusative. SIBAWAYH: Nominative forms such as night and day can be understood as apposition or as broad usage in which the time is treated as part of the expression. SIBAWAYH: Jarīr's verse treats night as a named part of the expression, supporting Sībawayh's broad nominative construction. SIBAWAYH: In the conditional examples, accusative follows one analysis, while nominative is possible when the clause means that truth or falsehood occurs or is present. SIBAWAYH: A pronoun may be clarified by an explicit body-part noun, as in the phrase about turning a back and belly; the poetry supplies parallel replacements. SIBAWAYH: Al-Jaʿdī's line permits أهلها

{"id": "2:61/q35", "question": "Which place does miṣr denote here?", "turns_on": "Tanwīn and proper-name grammar, the Holy Land command, and reports of later settlement.", "positions": [{"id": "2:61/q35/p1", "position": "An unspecified settled town or city", "reasons": "AKHFASH (بعضهم): Some distinguish the two occurrences: مصر in Joseph is the named Egypt, while مصر here means any city among cities. TAB-FULL: Most reciters pronounce miṣran with tanwīn; on this reading it means any town, since the requested crops are found in settled places rather than wilderness. TAB-FULL (قتادة): Qatada takes miṣran to mean one of the cities or towns. TAB-FULL (من قال إنها مصرا من الأمصار): Proponents of the generic-city reading argue that the Israelites were settled in Syria after leaving Egypt; the holy land was assigned to them, and their descendants entered it under Joshua after the forty years of wandering, with no text saying they returned to Egypt. ZAJJAJ: Most readers include final alif in “miṣran”; it can mean any town, appropriate to their wilderness setting, or Egypt as a masculine proper name and is then declinable. IBNABIHATIM (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas says “a town” means any one of the cities; al-Suddi, Qatada, and al-Rabi' agree. NAHHAS: مصرا is best read as indefinite, matching the written alif; taking مصر as a proper name is possible but less apt because it is called a town, not a land or country. THALABI (قتادة): Miṣr means any one of the cities: had the verse meant the particular Egypt, it would be uninflected, as in the command to enter Egypt in Joseph’s story. MAWARDI-FULL (قتادة): Qatada, al-Suddi, Mujahid, and Ibn Zayd say miṣran means any city, since the requested produce is available only in towns. WAHIDI-BASIT: With tanwin, Misran can mean any city, since the requested produce was available in towns and cities. JISHUMI (قراءة العامة): The common tanwīn on miṣran means any city; al-Ḥasan omits tanwīn to mean Egypt specifically, and Ibn Masʿūd’s codex lacks alif and tanwīn. JISHUMI (قتادة والسدي ومجاهد وأبو علي): Miṣran may mean any city; Abū ʿAlī argues it cannot mean Egypt because they were told to enter Jerusalem. BAGHAWI-FULL (الضحاك): Al-Dahhak identifies the city as the Egypt of Moses and Pharaoh; al-Baghawi prefers the generic meaning because the proper name Egypt would not take tanwīn. KASHSHAF-FULL: If it means the country, it has only one of the two causes of indeclinability; if it means any city, it is indefinite, while Abdullah's codex and al-Aʿmash read the city name without tanwin. IBNATIYYA-FULL (مجاهد وغيره ممن صرفها): Mujahid and others who inflect مصر take it as an unspecified town, citing the command to enter a town and reports that the Israelites settled Syria after the wilderness. TABRISI: All canonical readers give Miṣr tanwīn, taking it as an unspecified city since the Israelites were in the wilderness; it may instead mean Egypt proper, a masculine name. TABRISI (قتادة والسدي ومجاهد): Qatada, al-Suddi, and Mujahid take miṣr as any city: the requested crops are found in towns, not in the wilderness. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (ابن مسعود، ابن عباس، قتادة، ابن زيد): One view takes miṣran as any unspecified Egyptian city, since the requested produce was available in towns. RAZI-FULL (مفسرون): Among those accepting tanwin, some take Egypt to mean Pharaoh's country, while others understand it as any town where the requested foods could be found.
